Divorcement
dih-VORS-ment
noun
From the Latin divortium, “a turning apart,” through the Old French divorce, with the English suffix -ment denoting the act or the instrument of it; in the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew kērīthūth (a cutting off) and the Greek apostasion, the written deed of severance.

Biblical Definition

Divorcement is the formal putting away of a wife by a written deed. The word enters Scripture not as a gift but as a restraint: “then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house” (Deu 24:1). Moses did not institute the practice; he found it and bridled it, requiring a public document, a delivery into her hand, and a bar upon the first husband ever taking her again (Deu 24:4). The paper protected the woman and slowed the man. Our Lord Himself settles the question of what that statute meant. When the Pharisees pressed Him — “Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement?” (Mat 19:7) — He answered that Moses suffered it “because of the hardness of your hearts: but from the beginning it was not so” (Mat 19:8), and He sent them back past Sinai to Eden: one man, one woman, one flesh, and “what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6; Gen 2:24). A concession to hardness is not a licence to be hard. Isaiah turns the word to the LORD’s own use and demands the document be produced: “Where is the bill of your mother’s divorcement, whom I have put away?” (Isa 50:1). There is none, for He has not put His covenant people away; they sold themselves. The covenant God keeps is the pattern for the covenant of marriage.

Webster 1828 Definition

The legal dissolution of the marriage bond, and the written instrument by which it was declared; in Scripture a Mosaic restraint upon hardness of heart, not a permission.

expand to see more

DIVORCEMENT, dissolution of the bond of marriage; the act of putting away a wife, or the writing which declares it.

From the Latin divortium, a turning apart, from divertere, to turn aside.

In the Mosaic law the bill of divorcement was required in writing and delivered into the woman’s hand (Deu 24:1).

The word is used figuratively of the LORD’s dealings with Israel, whom He chastens but does not finally put away (Isa 50:1).

It is distinguished from separation, which suspends cohabitation without pretending to dissolve the bond.

Key Scripture

Deu 24:1 — "When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house."

Mat 19:8 — "He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so."

Mat 19:6 — "Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

Isa 50:1 — "Thus saith the LORD, Where is the bill of your mother's divorcement, whom I have put away? or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves, and for your transgressions is your mother put away."

Modern Corruption

No-fault divorce has taken a Mosaic restraint upon hardness of heart and made it the ordinary machinery of a culture that treats the marriage covenant as dissoluble at will.

expand to see more

The modern corruption is not that men divorce — men have always been hard — but that the law and the church together have stopped calling it what it is. The no-fault statutes that swept the American states from 1969 onward removed the requirement of any wrong at all: one party’s unwillingness now dissolves what two swore before God to keep. The governing phrase, irreconcilable differences, is a masterpiece of evasion; it names no sin, accuses no one, and quietly asserts that a covenant is a preference. Scripture will not have it. “For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away” (Mal 2:16), and the Lord Jesus grounds marriage not in the satisfaction of the parties but in the act of God: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6). Where Christ allows a narrow exception it is for fornication (Mat 19:9), and the apostle adds the desertion of an unbelieving spouse (1Co 7:15) — grounds, not moods. A marriage is not ended because it has ceased to please.

Notice also what the deed itself was for. The bill of divorcement was a burden laid on the man: he must write, and witness, and deliver, and he could never undo it and take her back (Deu 24:4). Moses put friction into the thing precisely because hard hearts move fast. Modern practice inverts the statute — the paperwork is now the easiest part of the transaction, filed online, uncontested, no cause alleged. And when the church absorbs that instinct and preaches divorce as an act of self-care, it is preaching the hardness Moses restrained. Recover the older order: marriage is one man and one woman covenanting before God for life (Gen 2:24); repentance and forgiveness are the ordinary remedy for the offences of a marriage; and the God who was provoked by Israel a thousand years and still would not produce the bill (Isa 50:1) is the pattern for husbands who have been sinned against.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kērīthūth, a cutting off; Greek apostasion, a standing away — both name a severance, and both are used of a written deed.

expand to see more

Hebrew kērīthūth (H3748) — a cutting, a severance; from kārath, to cut — the same verb used for cutting a covenant.

Greek apostasion (G647) — a standing off, hence the certificate of repudiation (Mat 5:31; Mat 19:7; Mar 10:4).

The Authorized Version renders the Hebrew phrase “bill of divorcement” and the Greek variously “writing of divorcement” and “bill of divorcement.”

That kārath both cuts a covenant and cuts one off is not accident: the same knife that binds can sever, and Scripture keeps the sobering echo.

Latin divortium underlies the English word — a turning apart of two who had gone one way.

Usage

"Of the Mosaic statute restraining a hard husband: the bill required, the woman protected, the return forbidden (Deu 24:1–4)."

"Of our Lord’s exposition, which sends the question back past Moses to the creation ordinance (Mat 19:4–9; Mar 10:2–12)."

"Figuratively of the LORD and His covenant people, where the demanded bill cannot be produced because He has not finally put her away (Isa 50:1)."
